primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Incontinentia pigmenti due to IKBKG dysfunction
mechanism: IKBKG encodes IKK-gamma/NEMO, the regulatory component of the IKK complex required for activation of NF-kappa-B. Loss of normal IKBKG function impairs NF-kappa-B-mediated survival signaling, increasing susceptibility to apoptosis and producing the X-linked dominant multisystem phenotype of incontinentia pigmenti.
vignette: A 3-month-old girl has recurrent vesicular skin lesions that evolved into verrucous plaques and then swirling hyperpigmentation along the lines of Blaschko. Ophthalmologic examination shows retinal vascular abnormalities. Genetic testing identifies a pathogenic variant in IKBKG.
lead: Which of the following signaling abnormalities most directly results from this mutation?
correct: Impaired activation of NF-kappa-B by the IKK complex, increasing susceptibility to apoptosis
distractors: Constitutive activation of the RAS-MAPK pathway
Failure of SMAD phosphorylation downstream of TGF-beta receptors
Excessive activation of JAK-STAT signaling by cytokine receptors
Failure of beta-catenin degradation in the Wnt signaling pathway
distractor_notes: Constitutive RAS-MAPK activation causes other developmental/cancer syndromes and is not the direct role of IKBKG/NEMO.
IKBKG is not a TGF-beta/SMAD signaling protein.
JAK-STAT hyperactivation is not the core molecular defect in incontinentia pigmenti.
Wnt/beta-catenin degradation machinery is distinct from the IKK/NF-kappa-B complex.
key_expl: IKBKG encodes NEMO/IKK-gamma, an essential regulatory component of the IKK complex. Without normal NEMO, NF-kappa-B activation is impaired; cells lose an important anti-apoptotic response, contributing to the characteristic X-linked dominant skin, dental, ocular, and neurologic manifestations.
objective: Identify defective IKBKG/NEMO-dependent NF-kappa-B activation as the molecular basis of incontinentia pigmenti.
clues: vesicular then verrucous then hyperpigmented lesions
